new_statements.quote: 8. (stress placement) In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase. Examples /tiŋaŋ/ → [ti'ŋãŋ] hornbill; /dara/ → [da'ra:] long, of time; /bəlatup/ → [bəla'tup] inflate; /kələsu/ → [kələ'su:] steam; /mata?+n do/ → ['mãtan do:] sun. [p. 76] — Stress, which falls on the final syllable of citation forms but on the penultimate syllable of forms in context in most of the languages described, provides probably the most conspicuous example of such a difference. [p. 33]
new_statements.citation: Blust, Robert A. 1977. Sketches of the morphology and phonology of Bornean languages 1: Uma Juman (Kayan). In C. Court, R. Blust & F. Watuseke (eds), Papers in Western Austronesian Linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-33), 7-122. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: p. 76, section 5.5.1 P-rule 8 '(stress placement)' (PDF page 82 of the ANU scan); supporting remark p. 33 (p. 39) and clitics p. 85 (p. 91)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and rendered p. 82 (printed p. 76) at 110 dpi: rule "8. (stress placement) In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase." followed by the five examples /tiŋaŋ/ → [ti'ŋãŋ] hornbill, /dara/ → [da'ra:] long, of time, /bəlatup/ → [bəla'tup] inflate, /kələsu/ → [kələ'su:] steam, /mata?+n do/ → ['mãtan do:] sun — exactly as quoted. The p. 33 (p. 39) sentence "Stress, which falls on the final syllable of citation forms but on the penultimate syllable of forms in context in most of the languages described, provides probably the most conspicuous example of such a difference" and the p. 85 (p. 91) remark that the locative clitic /ha?/ "is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In a word pronounced in isolation the final syllable (last vowel) carries stress; inside a phrase stress shifts to the penultimate syllable of the phrase, so non-final words in context lose their final stress (e.g. /duh aya?/ → [do'ha ya?] 'old woman', p. 85). Stress is not lexically contrastive; Blust treats it as a late phonological rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the transcriptions show one stress mark per phrase.
new_statements.exceptions: The generic locative clitic /ha?/ is never stressed in rapid speech and joins the following root as one phonological word (p. 85); monosyllabic function words are 'not normally stressed' while full words bear stress (p. 20 area, section on word classes).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form word domain gives final stress; phrase domain gives phrase-penultimate stress. Source describes Uma Juman, a Kayan dialect on the Balui branch of the Rejang river, Sarawak (Rejang Kayan, reja1241), from Blust's 1971 fieldwork — a sister lect of Mendalam Kayan, not Mendalam Kayan itself.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is for Uma Juman, a Kayan dialect of the Balui branch of the Rejang river, Sarawak, i.e. Rejang Kayan (Glottolog reja1241, ISO ree), not Mendalam Kayan (mend1267, West Kalimantan). It is a first-hand, well-located statement and would be a catalog candidate under reja1241; under mend1267 it is sister-lect evidence only. No Mendalam-specific phonological description could be opened: Hanye 1990 (the likely primary sketch; LC microfiche only) and Effendy 2006 (dictionary) exist but were not accessible, and the only Glottolog reference for mend1267 (Guerreiro 1996) is silent on stress.

sources.locator: p. 76, section 5.5.1 P-rule 8 '(stress placement)' (PDF page 82 of the ANU scan); supporting remark p. 33 (p. 39) and clitics p. 85 (p. 91)
sources.note: P-rule 8 'stress placement' (p. 76): in citation forms the last vowel of a word is stressed; within the phrase stress is penultimate; clitic /ha?/ never stressed (p. 85); p. 33 generalises final-in-citation / penultimate-in-context to most languages in the volume. Describes Uma Juman, a Kayan dialect of the Balui branch of the Rejang river, Sarawak (= Rejang Kayan reja1241), NOT Mendalam Kayan.

sources.citation: Guerreiro, Antonio J. 1996. Homophony, sound changes and dialectal variations in some central Bornean languages. Mon-Khmer Studies 25: 205-226.
sources.note: Comparative sound-change/lexical tables for Kayanic isolects; the only Glottolog reference for mend1267. Lists Kaya:n Menda:lam (Uma' Aging, Uma' Pagong, Uma' Suling, c.1,900 speakers) in Appendix I, p. 222. No statement on where word stress falls in any Kayan lect; the only stress mention (p. 212) is a general remark that unstressed /e/ drops in the drift toward monosyllabism (Modang, compared with Rade).

sources.note: The only known grammar sketch of the West-Kalimantan (= Mendalam) Kayan; Glottolog's hh.bib mis-guesses it as Baram Kayan, but the LC/OpenLibrary record says 'Kayan language spoken by Kayan tribe in Kalimantan Barat Province'.
